"Vikas, I'm telling you, Dev is trying to steal the Mehta project from me."
"Steal it how?"
"He keeps cc-ing the manager on every email. He wants her to think it was all him."
Vikas stirred his tea at the stall outside the office. "Did he say anything like that?"
"He doesn't need to. I just know."
"Okay. Can I ask you something weird?"
"What?"
"Have you thought about cc-ing her too?"
Pranav opened his mouth. Then shut it. "...Yes. All week, actually."
"So?"
Pranav stared at the traffic. "So maybe I'm the one who wants her to think it was me." He laughed, a bit embarrassed. "I just want her to see my part. She's never mentioned it once."
"Then tell her that. Straight. Not through Dev."
Pranav nodded slowly. The heat in his chest had gone.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Mateo slid Ivan's science worksheet across the lunch table and copied the answers onto his own. "You're copying?" Ivan asked. "Everyone copies," Mateo said. "Lucas copied yesterday. And Señora Paz gives us way too much. Three worksheets a week? That's crazy." He finished and handed it back. "Anyway, I knew most of it. I just didn't have time." That afternoon Señora Paz returned the worksheets. Mateo got a gold star. He looked at it for a long time. His mother always said he was the honest one in the family. He shoved the worksheet deep into his bag. At home, when his mother asked about school, he said, "Fine," and went straight to his room.

qa.q: What did Mateo get on the worksheet?
qa.a: A gold star.

qa.q: Why did Mateo shove the worksheet deep into his bag?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and guilty, because the gold star clashed with his picture of himself as the honest one.

qa.q: What could Mateo do to feel honest again?
qa.a: He could tell Señora Paz he copied and ask to redo the worksheet, or at least tell his mother what happened.

qa.q: What might Ivan be thinking about Mateo's reasons?
qa.a: Ivan might feel doubtful and a little used, since his worksheet was copied and the excuses came only after.

grounding: Shows a child who copied homework saying everyone does it and the teacher gives too much, reasons arriving after the act to protect his self-image.

passage: Arohi, you're telling me the test was unfair and marks don't matter? Ha. Come, let your Keerthana chithi tell you something. When I was fifteen, in Madurai, I didn't study for the half-yearly history exam. I was reading novels every night instead. The day before, I told everyone, "This exam is unfair. The syllabus is too long. And marks don't matter anyway; nobody asks your history marks in life." I felt so clever saying it. It made the shame go away, just for that evening. I got thirty-one. Then, in class eleven, I wanted history as my subject, and the school said my marks weren't high enough. I cried for a week. The story I told myself had felt good for one night and cost me a whole year. So now, tell me honestly, did you study?

qa.q: What mark did young Keerthana get in history?
qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: Why did saying the exam was unfair feel clever to young Keerthana?
qa.a: Young Keerthana felt ashamed about not studying, and the story made that shame go away for the evening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could Keerthana have done differently before it?
qa.a: Being refused history in class eleven; Keerthana could have admitted to not preparing and studied the chapters instead of blaming the exam.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Keerthana's speech about the unfair exam?
qa.a: Some might have agreed, while others who had studied might have seen it as an excuse.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager who didn't prepare deciding the exam was unfair and marks didn't matter, easing shame then but costing more later.

passage: In their Bhubaneswar flat, Kiran shut his maths book the night before the unit test. He hadn't opened it all week. "The test is unfair anyway," he told his mother, Rajni, when she came in with milk. "Mr Das puts questions from outside the syllabus. And unit tests don't even count much." Rajni sat on the bed. "When did you start revising?" Kiran looked at the book. "That's not the point." "What is the point?" He shrugged. His chest felt hot. It was easier to be angry at Mr Das than to admit he'd spent the week on his phone. Rajni didn't lecture. "Okay. Do the first chapter now. Just one. I'll sit here." Kiran sighed very loudly. But he opened the book.

qa.q: What subject was Kiran's unit test in?
qa.a: Maths.

qa.q: Why did Kiran say the test was unfair when his mother asked about revising?
qa.a: He felt ashamed about spending the week on his phone, and blaming the test and Mr Das felt easier than admitting it.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that helped Kiran without a lecture?
qa.a: She asked a simple question, then offered to sit with him while he did just one chapter.

qa.q: How might Mr Das see Kiran's claim about the syllabus?
qa.a: Mr Das might feel it was unfair to him, since the problem was that Kiran hadn't revised.

grounding: Shows a teenager who did not prepare deciding the test is unfair and doesn't count, easing shame now while raising the cost later.

passage: The week of Pallavi's sister's wedding was loud and full, and the power kept cutting out in the evenings. Nikita, staying with them, was supposed to revise for Monday's chemistry exam. She didn't open the book once. On Sunday night, in the candlelight, Pallavi asked, "Did you finish organic?" Nikita shrugged. "The chemistry teacher sets impossible papers. It's unfair. And it's just the half-yearly, it doesn't really matter." Pallavi raised an eyebrow. "You said the same about physics." Nikita laughed, but she felt a twist in her stomach. She knew she'd chosen mehendi and dancing over chemistry. Saying the paper was unfair made that feel less bad. "Want to do one chapter now?" Pallavi asked. "It's dark," Nikita said. Pallavi held up the candle.

qa.q: Which exam was on Monday?
qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel a twist in her stomach?
qa.a: She knew she had chosen the wedding fun over studying, and underneath the excuse she felt ashamed.

qa.q: What might help Nikita most tonight?
qa.a: Taking up Pallavi's offer to do one chapter by candlelight, so she lowers the cost on Monday instead of just easing the shame now.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Nikita's excuse?
qa.a: Pallavi seems unconvinced, pointing out Nikita said the same about physics and offering to study with her.

grounding: Shows a teenager who did not prepare deciding the exam is unfair and unimportant, lowering shame now while raising the cost later.

passage: In the office of the college scholarship cell in Nagpur, Suraj read the rejection letter twice, folded it, and turned to go. Professor Irawati, who ran the cell, caught him at the door. "Suraj, I'm sorry. Would you like feedback on your application?" "No need, ma'am. I never really wanted it. That exchange programme is overrated. Three months in a cold country, what's the use?" Professor Irawati nodded slowly. "You wrote four drafts of your essay." Suraj's jaw tightened. "That was just practice." "The panel had specific comments. They might help next year." "There won't be a next year. I'm not interested." He left. In the corridor, he took the letter out again and read the line "a strong candidate" three times. Then he put it away.

qa.q: How many drafts of the essay had Suraj written?
qa.a: Four drafts.

qa.q: Why did Suraj call the programme overrated?
qa.a: He felt deeply disappointed, and telling himself he never wanted it made the rejection hurt less.

qa.q: What could Suraj gain by accepting the feedback?
qa.a: He could learn what the panel thought, which might help next time, instead of hiding the chance to improve.

qa.q: How might Professor Irawati see Suraj's reaction?
qa.a: She likely sees the disappointment behind his words, since she knows he wrote four drafts, and hopes he'll come back for the feedback.

grounding: Shows a student turned down for a scholarship claiming he never wanted it, easing disappointment but refusing feedback that could help.

passage:
Subject: re: the scholarship

Vikas,

Yeah, I didn't get it. Honestly, I'm relieved. I never really wanted to go to Singapore for a semester. The whole programme is overrated. It's just a line on the CV. Everyone says the housing is terrible, and the course list is basically the same as ours.

Don't feel bad for me. I'm fine.

The email said I could book a feedback call with the committee. I'm not going to. What's the point, if I didn't want it anyway?

Anyway, are you coming for the match on Saturday?

Hemant

P.S. The girl who got it spent all summer on her project. So, whatever, good for her.

qa.q: Where would the scholarship semester have been?
qa.a: In Singapore.

qa.q: How does the P.S. hint at what Hemant really feels?
qa.a: The bitter "whatever, good for her" suggests Hemant feels disappointed and a little envious, despite claiming to be relieved.

qa.q: What would you advise Hemant about the feedback call?
qa.a: Book it anyway; hearing the committee's view could show what to change next time, even if it stings.

qa.q: How might Vikas read this email?
qa.a: Vikas may sense that Hemant is more hurt than he says, since the reasons for not wanting it arrived only after the rejection.

grounding: Shows a student turned down for a scholarship claiming never to have wanted it, easing disappointment while skipping a chance to learn.

passage: Farhan, you asked what happened with the music scholarship. Fine, Yash will tell you. I didn't get it. And you know what? Good. I never wanted it that much. The conservatory's so stiff. Everyone plays the same classical pieces. I'd have been bored. It's overrated, honestly. They sent an email offering feedback from the jury. I deleted it. Why would I want feedback on something I didn't care about? Although. I did practise that piece every morning at six for four months. Before college. My fingers were bleeding some days. So maybe I cared a little. But it's easier to say I didn't. If I say I didn't want it, then I didn't lose anything. Right? Anyway. Let's get chai. I'm fine.

qa.q: For how long did Yash practise the piece every morning?
qa.a: For four months.

qa.q: Why does Yash say the conservatory is overrated?
qa.a: Yash feels disappointed after months of hard practice, and saying it was never wanted makes the loss hurt less.

qa.q: What does Yash risk losing by deleting the jury's feedback?
qa.a: The chance to learn what could make the next attempt stronger, which the sour-grapes story hides.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel listening to this?
qa.a: Farhan might feel concerned and a little sad, noticing that Yash is clearly hurting under the "I'm fine."

grounding: Shows a student turned down for a scholarship saying they never wanted it, which eases disappointment but hides what could be learned.

passage: Rafiq, you want to know why I stopped trusting Vinay's explanations? It's me, Tejas, and I sit next to him. He promised the client report by Monday. Tuesday he told me the data was late. By Wednesday it was that the client changed the format. Thursday, the manager asked, and Vinay gave this long, beautiful explanation about server issues, the format, and a sick cousin. It was so smooth. Every detail fitted. That's what bothered me. The reasons kept changing, and each version was tidier than the last. I don't think he was lying, exactly. I think he felt bad and the story helped. So on Friday I didn't point out the changes. I just said, "Is something about this report hard? Want to go through it together?" He went quiet. Then: "I don't know how to do the analysis."

qa.q: By what day did Vinay promise the client report?
qa.a: By Monday.

qa.q: Why did Tejas find the smooth explanation more worrying than a messy one?
qa.a: Tejas felt uneasy because the reasons kept changing and getting tidier, which suggested something uncomfortable underneath rather than a simple delay.

qa.q: Which approach worked with Vinay, and why?
qa.a: Asking kindly whether the report was hard, instead of pointing out the changing stories, gave Vinay room to admit he didn't know the analysis.

qa.q: How might Vinay feel when Tejas offers to go through it together?
qa.a: Vinay might feel relieved and a bit ashamed, finally able to drop the explanations and ask for help.

grounding: Shows a colleague hearing a peer's shifting, tidy excuses for a missed promise and reading the smoothness as a clue to discomfort underneath.

passage: I'm Lavanya, and I work two desks from Samir at the design studio in Chennai. I don't know what's going on inside him; I can only say what I saw. On Monday he promised the logo drafts to the client by Wednesday. Wednesday came, and he told the team lead the brief had changed. At lunch he told me the printer had broken. On Friday he told the client it was a font licence issue. Each time, he spoke fast and at length, with lots of detail, smiling. It was very convincing. But the reasons didn't match. I noticed he wouldn't open the file when anyone was nearby. I didn't say anything to the team lead. On Friday evening I just asked him, "Are you stuck on it? I'm free Saturday morning." He looked at his screen for a long time.

qa.q: What reason did Samir give Lavanya at lunch?
qa.a: The printer had broken.

qa.q: What made Lavanya suspect something uncomfortable underneath Samir's explanations?
qa.a: Lavanya felt uneasy because the reasons kept changing and he spoke fast and at length, and he avoided opening the file when others were near.

qa.q: Why was offering Saturday morning a wise response?
qa.a: It gives Samir a kind, low-pressure way to admit he is stuck, instead of catching him out in front of the team lead.

qa.q: How might Samir feel when Lavanya asks if he's stuck?
qa.a: Samir might feel exposed but also relieved, as his long silence suggests the question touched the real problem.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's account, noticing a peer's changing and tidy reasons for a slipped promise as a clue to discomfort underneath.

passage:
Monday. In the stand-up, Jatin said the website testing would be done by Wednesday. He sounded confident.
Wednesday. Jatin explained, at length, that the test server was down. He had a whole story about a vendor, a password reset and a public holiday in another country. Jahnavi, who sat across from him, nodded, but something felt off. The server had been fine when she used it that morning.
Friday. The manager asked again. Jatin gave a new reason: the requirements had been unclear. He spoke for three minutes, smooth, with charts. Jahnavi noticed the story had changed completely. She didn't say so in the meeting. Afterwards, at the coffee machine, she said, "The testing seems to be giving you a hard time. Is there a bit you're not sure how to do?" Jatin stirred his coffee. "Automation," he said finally. "I've never done it."

qa.q: What did Jatin say was down on Wednesday?
qa.a: The test server.

qa.q: Why did something feel off to Jahnavi on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt doubtful because the server had worked for her that morning, and Jatin's story was long and detailed in a way that seemed too neat.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi respond without shaming Jatin?
qa.a: She waited until after the meeting and privately asked if there was a part he wasn't sure how to do.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel admitting he has never done automation?
qa.a: Jatin probably feels embarrassed but relieved to finally say the real problem.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a peer's changing, smooth reasons for a slipped promise across several days and reading them as a sign of discomfort underneath.
